title: Cardiovascular Prevention: Treat Absolute Risk, Not One Risk Factor
bottomLine: Cardiovascular prevention is risk-based and cumulative. Identify established ASCVD and statin-indicated/high-risk conditions first, then integrate blood pressure, lipids, diabetes, kidney disease, smoking, physical activity, diet, weight, pregnancy-related risk history and social barriers into one prevention plan rather than treating each number in isolation.
recognize: Established ASCVD is secondary prevention and changes treatment intensity immediately.
CKD, diabetes, smoking, severe dyslipidemia, family history and selected pregnancy-related conditions can materially change lifetime cardiovascular risk.
differentiate: A low short-term risk estimate does not erase very high LDL/familial hypercholesterolemia or established vascular disease.
Primary prevention and secondary prevention use different evidence thresholds and urgency.
assessment: Assess BP quality, lipids, diabetes/kidney status, smoking/vaping, family/premature disease, pregnancy complications, diet/activity, sleep, alcohol, medication access and readiness for change.
workup: Use a validated Canadian risk approach when applicable and obtain cause-directed testing for severe dyslipidemia, secondary hypertension or other unusual patterns.
Do not use indiscriminate cardiac imaging as a substitute for standard risk assessment.
management: Treat all major modifiable risks together with evidence-based pharmacotherapy and health-behaviour support.
Prioritize absolute risk reduction and therapies with proven cardiovascular outcome benefit rather than chasing isolated surrogate targets.
medicationSafety: Review pregnancy potential, kidney/liver function, drug interactions and bleeding/hypoglycemia risks before prevention medications.
Avoid adding aspirin for routine primary prevention without an individualized benefit-harm assessment.
redFlags: Symptoms suggesting active ischemia or vascular disease
Severe uncontrolled hypertension with organ injury
counselling: Use non-stigmatizing shared decision-making and explain absolute benefit, not only relative-risk percentages.
Address cost, food access, transportation and medication coverage as treatment variables.
followUp: Reassess BP, lipid/diabetes response, adherence/tolerance and lifestyle goals after clinically meaningful changes.
examTrap: Focusing on a mildly high LDL in a low-risk patient while under-treating a patient with established ASCVD whose LDL looks 'not that bad'.
oneLinePearl: Prevent cardiovascular events by treating total risk, not the loudest single number.
sourceBasis: Canadian Cardiovascular Society prevention and dyslipidemia resources

title: After MI: Secondary Prevention Starts Before the Patient Leaves
bottomLine: Surviving an MI is the start of long-term ASCVD care. Confirm the antithrombotic plan, intensive lipid lowering, BP/diabetes/smoking management, indicated beta-blocker/RAAS/HF therapy, cardiac rehabilitation, activity/work/driving guidance and closed-loop follow-up before assuming the acute event is 'finished'.
recognize: Medication omissions, early discontinuation, residual smoking, untreated lipids/BP/diabetes and failure to access cardiac rehabilitation create preventable recurrent risk.
New/recurrent chest pain, HF, arrhythmia or bleeding after discharge changes the pathway from routine follow-up to urgent reassessment.
differentiate: Secondary prevention is not just a statin prescription; it includes antithrombotic duration, lifestyle/rehab, ventricular-function/HF management and access/adherence.
Routine long-term dual antiplatelet therapy duration is individualized to ischemic and bleeding risk rather than a universal forever rule.
assessment: Review infarct/revascularization details, LV function, residual symptoms, antithrombotics, lipid/BP/diabetes control, smoking, bleeding, renal function, psychosocial recovery and medication access.
workup: Follow post-MI testing based on LV function, symptoms, arrhythmia and revascularization plan; do not repeat ischemia testing routinely without a clinical question.
management: Use the CCS post-ACS secondary-prevention pathway, including high-intensity lipid lowering and evidence-based cardioprotective therapy matched to comorbidity.
Refer/ensure cardiac rehabilitation and structured return-to-activity/work planning.
medicationSafety: Antithrombotic combinations require bleeding-risk and interaction review.
ACEi/ARB/ARNI, MRA and other HF/post-MI therapy require renal, potassium and BP monitoring when indicated.
redFlags: Medication interruption after recent PCI without cardiology input
counselling: Teach emergency symptom response, medication purpose, smoking cessation, rehab benefit and that feeling better does not mean recurrence risk has disappeared.
followUp: Use early closed-loop primary-care/cardiology follow-up to reconcile medications, lipids, BP, function, bleeding and rehab participation.
examTrap: Discharging a post-MI patient with medications but no cardiac-rehabilitation or secondary-prevention follow-up plan.
oneLinePearl: The post-MI treatment plan begins at discharge and continues for life.
sourceBasis: Canadian Cardiovascular Society Secondary Prevention Pathway

title: HFrEF Titration: Build the Four Pillars, Then Optimize Safely
bottomLine: For suitable HFrEF patients, initiate the four foundational disease-modifying classes early and titrate toward target or maximally tolerated therapy with deliberate BP, renal, potassium, volume and symptom monitoring. Do not spend months maximizing one class while the others are absent without a clinical reason.
recognize: ARNI/ACEi/ARB, evidence-based beta blocker, MRA and SGLT2 inhibitor form the current foundational HFrEF regimen for most eligible patients.
Loop diuretics relieve congestion but do not replace disease-modifying therapy.
differentiate: A creatinine change after RAAS/SGLT2 initiation is interpreted in clinical context; not every small rise means the drug must be permanently stopped.
Beta-blocker titration in stable euvolemic chronic HF differs from treatment of shock/severe acute decompensation.
assessment: Assess BP/orthostasis, heart rate/rhythm, volume status, renal function/eGFR, potassium, symptoms, adherence/cost and recent decompensation.
workup: Check renal function/potassium after clinically meaningful RAAS/ARNI/MRA changes according to patient risk and local practice; monitor glycemic/volume effects and adverse events for SGLT2 inhibitors.
management: Sequence/parallel-initiate foundational therapies as tolerated, then titrate and add indicated agents for persistent symptoms/rhythm/iron deficiency or other specific needs.
Reassess EF after optimized/maximally tolerated therapy when device candidacy depends on persistent systolic dysfunction.
medicationSafety: Do not combine ACE inhibitor with ARNI without the required washout or use ACEi+ARB routinely.
SGLT2 inhibitors need sick-day/perioperative counselling; MRA/RAAS therapy requires potassium/renal surveillance.
counselling: Explain each drug's survival/hospitalization role so patients understand why multiple classes are used even when they feel better.
followUp: Use frequent early titration reviews until a stable maximally tolerated regimen is reached, then monitor symptoms, renal/electrolytes and adherence longitudinally.
examTrap: Maximizing the beta blocker for months before starting the other foundational HFrEF classes in a stable eligible patient.
oneLinePearl: HFrEF optimization is about getting all four pillars on board safely, then titrating—not perfecting one pillar first.
sourceBasis: Canadian Heart Failure Society practical tools

title: Pacemakers, ICDs, and CRT: Match the Device to the Risk
bottomLine: Pacemakers treat clinically important brady/conduction disease; ICDs prevent sudden arrhythmic death in selected high-risk patients; CRT treats selected electrical/mechanical dyssynchrony in HF. Device decisions follow documented rhythm, symptoms, EF/QRS context, optimized therapy and goals—not 'low heart rate' or 'low EF' alone.
recognize: Symptomatic high-grade AV block and selected sinus-node disease are pacing problems.
Persistently reduced LVEF despite optimized/maximally tolerated GDMT can trigger ICD/CRT assessment depending on rhythm, QRS and overall prognosis.
differentiate: A pacemaker does not treat ventricular-fibrillation risk unless combined ICD capability is indicated.
ICD/CRT benefit depends on competing non-arrhythmic mortality and patient goals; very limited prognosis can change candidacy.
assessment: Assess documented brady/tachy rhythm, syncope, conduction pattern, EF, QRS morphology/duration, HF status, reversible causes, prior VT/VF and goals of care.
workup: Use ECG/rhythm monitoring and echo as indicated; reassess EF after target/maximally tolerated HFrEF therapy before primary-prevention ICD/CRT referral when feasible.
management: Refer appropriate patients to electrophysiology/device services and do not delay urgent pacing in unstable high-grade block while waiting for elective workup.
Continue disease-modifying HF/rhythm therapy after implantation unless a specific reason changes the plan.
medicationSafety: Correct reversible drug/electrolyte bradyarrhythmia before permanent-device decisions when clinically safe.
Device implantation does not remove the need to review anticoagulation, antiarrhythmics or HF medications.
counselling: Explain what the device can and cannot do, shock response, wound/device follow-up, electromagnetic precautions and individualized driving restrictions.
followUp: Ensure device-clinic/remote monitoring, wound review and ongoing HF/rhythm reassessment.
examTrap: Referring immediately for a primary-prevention ICD at the moment HFrEF is diagnosed before giving suitable GDMT a chance to improve EF when the patient is stable enough to do so.
oneLinePearl: Choose the device for the documented electrical/sudden-death problem, not the diagnosis label alone.
sourceBasis: Canadian Cardiovascular Society 2021 HFrEF device referral guidance
Canadian Heart Rhythm Society device resources

title: Endocarditis Prophylaxis: Reserve Antibiotics for the Highest-Risk Cardiac Patients
bottomLine: Antibiotic prophylaxis before dental procedures is reserved for selected highest-risk cardiac conditions undergoing procedures that manipulate gingival/periapical tissue or perforate oral mucosa. Routine murmurs, uncomplicated MVP and most native valve disease do not justify prophylaxis.
recognize: Prior infective endocarditis, selected prosthetic valves/material and certain high-risk congenital/transplant-associated lesions drive prophylaxis eligibility.
Good oral health and prompt evaluation of unexplained bacteremia/fever matter more broadly than prophylaxis for low-risk lesions.
differentiate: Endocarditis prophylaxis eligibility is not the same as needing antibiotics for an active dental infection.
Most GI/GU procedures do not require cardiac endocarditis prophylaxis solely because heart disease is present.
assessment: Verify the exact cardiac lesion/device, prior endocarditis, planned dental procedure, antibiotic allergy and current infection.
workup: No testing is required merely to 'prove' prophylaxis need; use the current cardiac condition/procedure criteria and confirm uncertain complex congenital/transplant cases with cardiology.
management: Give the current recommended prophylactic regimen only when both cardiac-risk and procedure criteria are met.
Do not broaden or extend antibiotics beyond the prophylaxis recommendation without another infection indication.
medicationSafety: Check true beta-lactam allergy/anaphylaxis history and current recommendations rather than automatically choosing older alternatives.
Unnecessary prophylaxis contributes to adverse drug reactions and antimicrobial resistance.
redFlags: Embolic/heart-failure signs concerning for active endocarditis
counselling: Explain why most valve conditions no longer need prophylaxis and emphasize oral hygiene and prompt assessment of persistent unexplained fever.
followUp: Document the exact prophylaxis indication so future clinicians do not repeatedly reconstruct it from a vague 'heart murmur' history.
examTrap: Prescribing dental prophylaxis for uncomplicated mitral valve prolapse or an innocent murmur.
oneLinePearl: Endocarditis prophylaxis is for a small high-risk group—not every structural heart diagnosis.

title: Statins: Match Intensity to Risk and Monitor Clinically
bottomLine: Statin choice/intensity follows ASCVD risk and indication, not LDL alone. Use maximally tolerated evidence-based therapy for secondary prevention/high-risk states, check response/adherence, and investigate clinically significant muscle/hepatic symptoms rather than ordering routine CK/liver panels forever in asymptomatic stable patients.
recognize: Established ASCVD generally warrants intensive lipid lowering unless contraindicated or inconsistent with goals of care.
Severe LDL elevation/familial hypercholesterolemia, diabetes and CKD can create treatment indications independent of short-term risk.
differentiate: Statin-associated symptoms require timing, rechallenge/alternative causes and interaction review; one episode of nonspecific muscle pain does not automatically equal permanent intolerance.
OTC fish oil/supplements are not equivalent to evidence-based prescription lipid therapy.
assessment: Assess ASCVD/overall risk, prior statin response, pregnancy potential, liver disease, interacting drugs, alcohol, hypothyroidism/muscle disease and patient concerns.
workup: Use baseline lipids and repeat after initiation/intensification to assess response/adherence.
Check CK/liver tests when symptoms/risk factors make them clinically indicated rather than as reflex recurring surveillance.
management: Use guideline-directed statin intensity and add nonstatin therapy when residual risk/LDL thresholds warrant it despite maximally tolerated statin.
Use structured re-challenge/alternate statin/dosing strategies when intolerance is plausible rather than abandoning therapy prematurely.
medicationSafety: Review major CYP/transporter interactions and pregnancy/planning pregnancy.
Severe weakness with marked CK/renal injury or jaundice requires urgent evaluation rather than routine outpatient dose adjustment.
redFlags: Recurrent ASCVD despite apparently adequate therapy
counselling: Explain absolute cardiovascular benefit and distinguish common aches from true serious statin toxicity.
followUp: Track lipids, adherence, symptoms and overall prevention plan; do not measure treatment success from LDL alone if other risks remain uncontrolled.
examTrap: Stopping statin therapy permanently after one episode of nonspecific myalgia without checking interactions, thyroid disease or a re-challenge strategy.
oneLinePearl: Use the most effective statin the patient can safely sustain—and manage intolerance rather than surrendering prevention.
